Luke Morken
Team Lead & Project Author

As is stand, we cannot enforce OS-level enforcement for the EduQuest. In order to do so we would need to submit an application to Apple and Android and have them review EduQuest for it get permission. We do not have the time or resources to do that. For this product we will make it without the OS-level enforcement with the idea of expanding upon EduQuest’s capabilities. Without the OS-level enforcement, we cannot prevent children from uninstalling EduQuest. Nor can prevent kids from using devices with a set limit. EduQuest will operate as a standalone app that the children will have to interact with willingly and to do questions on their own. This presentation is made based on the idea that we DO have permission and the capability to use OS-level enforcement.
Children spend a lot of time using entertainment screens, displacing time that could be used to reinforce academic skills.
Fixed Screen Time → Questions Mode → Answer Questions → Earn More Screen Time
EduQuest turns recreational screen time into an opportunity for learning by requiring children to answer short educational questions before entertainment apps unlock.

Reading and math scores among 9-year-old students have dropped to their lowest levels in decades . 
At the same time, children ages 8 to 12 average approximately 5.5 hours of recreational screen time each day, it displaces valuable time that could be otherwise be used to reinforce foundation skills
1 National Center for Education Statistics (See References A) 2 Rideout, Victoria, et al. (See References A)
The challenge is not simply how much screen time children have, but how that time is being used.
> 4 hours daily video/gaming vs. 9 minutes e-reading.¹
47% of parents struggle to manage screen time for their children.²
Only 19% of parents consistently follow their children's screen time rules.²
¹ Rideout et al. (See Reference A) | ² Pew Research. (See Reference G)
Parent Sets Screen Time Limits With Existing Tools
Child Waits Or Ask For More Time
The current process simply restricts time usage, resulting in a missed opportunity for learning and zero educational reinforcement.

EduQuest is a mobile application controlled by parents that combines screen time management with educational practice. 
The application allows parents to set screen-time limits and requires children to complete age appropriate questions to earn additional screen time. Parents are also able to monitor learning progress over time.

Children answer age-appropriate reading and math questions.
Completed questions earn additional recreational screen time.
Parents monitor question performance, screen-time activity, and learning progress.
EduQuest supports practice and reinforcement, but it will not replace teachers, schools, or formal instruction.
EduQuest will not completely block recreational screen use. It is designed to encourage a balance between learning and entertainment.
Parents will still decide appropriate screen-time limits and manage their child’s settings.
EduQuest can encourage educational practice, but it cannot guarantee academic improvement.

Appendix A: Key Terms & Concepts
Recreational Screen Time  Time spent using a device for fun, such as playing games, watching videos, or using social media.
Screen-Time Management  Tools used to track or limit how much time someone spends on a device or app.
Parent Dashboard  A screen where parents can view and manage their child's activity and learning progress.
Adaptive Learning  A learning method that changes based on how well a student is doing.
Content Filtering  Tools that block or limit access to certain apps, websites, or other digital content.
Cross-Platform  Software that can work on more than one type of device or operating system.
Ecosystem-Locked  Software that only works within one company's devices or services.

Appendix B: Basic Technical Terms
Frontend  The part of an app that users see and interact with.
Backend  The part of an app that works behind the scenes to process information and make features work.
Relational Database  A database that stores information in tables that can be connected to each other.
Server Framework  A set of tools developers use to build the part of an app that runs on a server.
API (Application Programming Interface)  A tool that allows different programs or parts of an app to communicate with each other.
Screen Time API  Apple tools that allow an app to work with screen-time controls on Apple devices.
Device Administration API  Android tools that allow an app to manage certain settings and controls on a device.

Appendix C: Development Technologies 
Linux  An operating system often used to run servers and online services.
Python  A programming language that can be used to build the behind-the-scenes parts of an app.
Swift  A programming language used to build software for Apple devices.
Kotlin  A programming language commonly used to build Android apps.
PostgreSQL  A database system used to store and organize information.
FastAPI  A Python tool used to build the backend of an application.
Django  A Python tool used to build websites and the backend of applications.

React Native  A tool that lets developers build mobile apps for both iOS and Android.
Flutter  A tool that lets developers build apps for different types of devices using the same code.
Docker  A tool that packages an application with the things it needs to run.
Container  A package that holds an application and the files and tools it needs to run.
Containerized Deployment  Running an application using containers so it works the same way in different environments.
Firebase Cloud Messaging  A service used to send notifications and messages to mobile devices.

Appendix D: Development Process
IDE (Integrated Development Environment)  A program developers use to write, edit, and work with computer code.
Version Control  A system that keeps track of changes made to computer code over time.
Git  A version-control tool used to track changes made to code.
GitHub  An online service where teams can store code and work on it together.
CI/CD (Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery)  A process that helps teams automatically test, build, and prepare new code for release.
GitHub Actions  A GitHub tool that can automatically run tasks such as testing or building code.
Workflow  A set of steps or tasks that are completed in a certain order.

Appendix E: Security & Data Terms 
Authentication  Checking that someone really is who they say they are.
Authorization  Deciding what a user is allowed to see or do after they sign in.
Encryption  Protecting information by changing it into a form that unauthorized people cannot easily read.
Data Access  The ability to view, use, or change stored information.
Data Collection  Gathering and storing information from or about users.
Parental Authorization  Permission from a parent or guardian for a child's account or use of certain features.
